title: Hydrocarbons

toc.title: 17.1 Cracking, pyrolysis and reforming; petrol quality, octane and cetane numbers and additives
17.2 Alkanes, alkenes and alkynes: isomerism, nomenclature and preparation; properties of ethane; additions and alkyne acidity
17.3 Aromaticity and resonance; preparation and properties of benzene

html:
Hydrocarbons are the carbon skeletons on which the rest of organic chemistry is built, and they contribute about 3 questions.

The paper moves quickly from fuels to reaction patterns: first how refineries reshape molecules for engines, then how σ-bonded alkanes, π-bonded alkenes/alkynes and the delocalized benzene ring each react.

Keep one mechanistic question in front of you — where are the available electrons? Alkanes hide them in strong σ bonds, alkenes and alkynes offer π electrons to electrophiles, and benzene offers π electrons but fights to keep its aromatic sextet.

What the paper asks from this chapter
  • Cracking breaks long hydrocarbons into shorter, more useful alkanes and alkenes. Pyrolysis is thermal decomposition without oxygen; steam cracking is high-temperature pyrolysis used especially for ethene/propene. Reforming rearranges/cyclizes/aromatizes straight chains to improve petrol quality and make BTX aromatics plus H₂.
  • Octane number measures resistance to knocking in a spark-ignition engine: 2,2,4-trimethylpentane (“isooctane”) = 100, n-heptane = 0. It is not a measure of energy content. Cetane number measures diesel ignition quality (short ignition delay): n-hexadecane = 100. Straight chains tend to have low octane but high cetane.
  • Tetraethyllead was the historic antiknock additive, now abandoned as a neurotoxic pollutant and catalyst poison. Modern blending uses branched alkylate, reformate, aromatics within limits and oxygenates such as ethanol; MTBE has groundwater-contamination concerns.
  • Alkanes (CₙH₂ₙ₊₂) are tetrahedral, nonpolar and comparatively inert. Main reactions: combustion, free-radical halogenation, pyrolysis/cracking, isomerization and aromatization. Ethane burns, undergoes UV chlorination and cracks to ethene + H₂.
  • Prepare alkanes by catalytic hydrogenation, Wurtz coupling (2 RX + 2 Na in dry ether; symmetrical products), decarboxylation of sodium carboxylates with soda lime (one carbon fewer) and reduction of alkyl halides.
  • Alkenes (CₙH₂ₙ) are planar at C=C and show chain/position and E/Z isomerism. Prepare by alcohol dehydration, dehydrohalogenation with alcoholic KOH, Zn dehalogenation of vicinal dihalides and stereoselective partial hydrogenation of alkynes.
  • Alkene additions: H₂/catalyst; X₂ (decolorized); HX by Markovnikov orientation through the more stable carbocation; HBr/peroxide by a radical anti-Markovnikov path; cold dilute alkaline KMnO₄ to a cis-diol; ozonolysis cleaves C=C to carbonyls; acid hydration gives Markovnikov alcohol.
  • Alkynes (CₙH₂ₙ₋₂) are linear at C≡C. Prepare ethyne from CaC₂ + water or by double dehydrohalogenation. Lindlar H₂ gives a cis-alkene; Na/liquid NH₃ gives a trans-alkene. Hydration (HgSO₄/H₂SO₄) gives an enol that tautomerizes: ethyne → ethanal, a terminal alkyne → methyl ketone.
  • A terminal alkyne C–H is weakly acidic (pKₐ ≈ 25) because the conjugate base holds its lone pair in an sp orbital (50% s). It forms metal acetylides with Na/NaNH₂, white Ag acetylide with ammoniacal AgNO₃ and red Cu(I) acetylide with ammoniacal Cu₂Cl₂.
  • Benzene is a planar regular hexagon with six equal C–C bonds (≈139 pm) and a cyclic 6π cloud. Hückel aromaticity requires a cyclic, planar, fully conjugated system with 4n+2 π electrons. Benzene prefers electrophilic substitution over addition because substitution restores aromaticity. Key electrophiles: NO₂⁺ (nitration), polarized X₂/FeX₃ (halogenation), SO₃ (sulfonation), R⁺ or RCO⁺ equivalents with AlCl₃ (Friedel–Crafts).

17.1 Cracking, pyrolysis and reforming; petrol quality, octane and cetane numbers and additives

Crude oil fractions seldom match market demand or engine design. Refineries therefore perform molecular tailoring.

Cracking uses heat and/or a catalyst to split a long-chain hydrocarbon into shorter molecules. A representative split is

C₁₆H₃₄ → C₈H₁₈ + C₈H₁₆.

Catalytic cracking over acidic zeolites gives branched, high-octane petrol components and valuable propene/butenes. Hydrocracking adds H₂ over a catalyst and gives more saturated, cleaner middle distillates.

Pyrolysis is decomposition by heat in the absence (or near-absence) of oxygen. In petrochemistry, steam cracking of ethane, propane or naphtha at roughly 800–900 °C for a fraction of a second maximizes ethene and propene for polymers.

Even a simple alkane can be described by several competing pyrolyses; for ethane the headline dehydrogenation is

C₂H₆ → C₂H₄ + H₂.

Reforming does not mainly shorten the chain. Over Pt/Re catalysts at high temperature, straight-chain alkanes isomerize to branched alkanes and cyclize/dehydrogenate to aromatics. For example,

n-C₇H₁₆ → C₆H₅CH₃ + 4H₂,

and n-hexane can be aromatized to benzene (also §17.3). Reformate has high octane; the H₂ co-product feeds refinery hydroprocessing.

In older school language, “reforming” may also describe converting straight-chain petrol hydrocarbons into branched ones — the goal is the same shape change.

Octane: resistance to unwanted self-ignition

In a petrol engine the spark should start a smooth flame front. Knocking is the damaging, near-explosive autoignition of the unburned mixture ahead of that front.

The octane scale assigns 100 to very knock-resistant 2,2,4-trimethylpentane and 0 to knock-prone n-heptane. A fuel rated 95 behaves, in the test engine, like a 95:5 blend of those reference compounds.

Laboratory RON and the harsher MON differ, but the examination point is simple: higher octane permits higher compression without knock; it does not automatically mean more energy per litre.

Branched alkanes, cycloalkanes, many aromatics and ethanol-rich blends resist knock better than long straight chains.

Tetraethyllead, Pb(C₂H₅)₄, once quenched radical pre-flame chemistry at tiny concentration, but it spread lead through cities (Ch. 15), poisoned catalytic converters and has been removed from road petrol worldwide.

Present-day octane comes from refinery streams and additives/blendstocks: alkylate, reformate, isomerate, ethanol and other ether oxygenates where permitted.

MTBE raises octane and oxygen content but its taste/odour and mobility in groundwater led many jurisdictions to restrict it.

Detergents, antioxidants and metal deactivators are fuel additives too, but they manage deposits and storage rather than the octane scale itself.

Cetane: willingness to ignite on compression

A diesel engine has no spark: injected fuel must ignite promptly in hot compressed air.

Cetane number measures that readiness — higher cetane means shorter ignition delay, smoother start and less diesel knock. n-Hexadecane (old name cetane) is 100.

The structural preference is opposite to petrol: a long straight chain autoignites readily, so it has high cetane but poor octane. Cetane improvers such as 2-ethylhexyl nitrate decompose to radicals that shorten ignition delay.

Two engines, opposite wishes

Spark engine: “wait for the spark” — high octane. Diesel: “ignite when squeezed, at once” — high cetane. A straight-chain molecule obeys the diesel wish and disobeys the petrol wish.

Pricing the pump

Problem. A petrol sample knocks exactly like a blend of 92 % iso-octane and 8 % n-heptane by volume. State its octane number, and name two modern additives that could raise it without lead.

If a diesel matches 65 % cetane with 35 % α-methylnaphthalene, what is its cetane number?

Solution. Octane number = the iso-octane percentage of the matching blend = 92; lead-free boosters include ethanol and MTBE (or reformate aromatics). Cetane number = the cetane percentage = 65.

The two scales run opposite temperaments: petrol wants reluctance to auto-ignite, diesel wants eagerness — one barrel, two contradictory virtues.

17.2 Alkanes, alkenes and alkynes: isomerism, nomenclature and preparation; properties of ethane; additions and alkyne acidity

Structures and isomerism at a glance

Family Bonding/geometry Isomerism to watch
Alkane, CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ sp³, tetrahedral; rotation about σ bonds gives conformers, not new structural isomers Chain isomerism begins at C₄; a substituted alkane frequent trap is missing a branched parent
Alkene, CₙH₂ₙ sp², trigonal planar at C=C; π bond blocks rotation Chain and position isomerism; cycloalkanes are ring–chain functional isomers; E/Z when each C=C carbon has two different groups
Alkyne, CₙH₂ₙ₋₂ sp, linear at C≡C; two π bonds Chain/position isomerism; dienes and cycloalkenes share the formula; terminal vs internal controls acidity tests

Nomenclature follows Ch. 16: longest chain including the multiple bond, lowest locant to the multiple bond, ene before yne when a genuine tie must be broken, and E/Z descriptors when a stereoisomer is specified.

CH₃–C(CH₃)=CH–CH₃ is 2-methylbut-2-ene; CH≡C–CH(CH₃)₂ is 3-methylbut-1-yne.

Preparation of alkanes and the chemistry of ethane

  • Catalytic hydrogenation: an alkene or alkyne with H₂/Ni, Pt or Pd gives the alkane.
  • Wurtz reaction: 2CH₃CH₂Br + 2Na →(dry ether) CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃ + 2NaBr. It joins two identical alkyl groups efficiently; two different halides give a mixture, and methane cannot be made this way.
  • Decarboxylation: soda lime (NaOH + CaO) removes the carboxyl carbon: CH₃CO₂Na + NaOH → CH₄ + Na₂CO₃. The alkane has one carbon fewer than the acid salt.
  • Reduction of alkyl halides: Zn/acid and other reducing systems replace halogen by H.
  • Kolbe electrolysis of a concentrated carboxylate can couple two alkyl radicals at the anode, a laboratory route to symmetrical even-carbon alkanes.

Ethane is a colourless, odourless, sparingly soluble gas (b.p. −89 °C). It burns completely,

2C₂H₆ + 7O₂ → 4CO₂ + 6H₂O,

and in oxygen-poor flames gives CO/soot. With Cl₂ in sunlight/UV it undergoes free-radical substitution,

C₂H₆ + Cl₂ → C₂H₅Cl + HCl,

with further chlorination possible. The chain has initiation (Cl₂ → 2Cl•), propagation (Cl• abstracts H, then C₂H₅• reacts with Cl₂) and termination (two radicals combine).

Bromination is slower and more selective in higher alkanes; direct iodination is unfavourable because HI reduces the alkyl iodide back.

Hot concentrated HNO₃ vapour can nitrate alkanes (radical nitration), and strong heating cracks/pyrolyses them.

Rotation about ethane's C–C bond interconverts staggered (lower energy) and eclipsed conformations; they are not separable isomers at room temperature.

Alkanes generally have low density, are insoluble in water and show boiling point rising with chain length. Branching lowers boiling point by making molecules more compact and reducing contact area/dispersion forces.

Their old name paraffins (“little affinity”) fits their indifference to acids, alkalis and ordinary oxidants: only strong σ bonds are offered and there is no accessible π bond or lone pair.

Preparation and addition chemistry of alkenes

Alkenes are made by elimination: dehydration of an alcohol with hot concentrated H₂SO₄ or Al₂O₃; dehydrohalogenation of an alkyl halide with hot alcoholic KOH; and Zn dehalogenation of a vicinal dihalide.

When two β-hydrogens can be removed unequally, the Saytzeff (Zaitsev) product — the more substituted, more stable alkene — usually dominates.

Partial hydrogenation of an alkyne with Lindlar catalyst adds H₂ syn to give the cis-alkene; Na in liquid NH₃ gives the trans-alkene.

The π bond is the reactive handle. Typical electrophilic addition begins when the π electrons attack E⁺, placing the new bond so that the more stable carbocation forms; a nucleophile then completes the product.

That mechanism is the reason behind Markovnikov's rule for HX: hydrogen attaches to the alkene carbon already richer in hydrogen because protonation at the other carbon gives the better carbocation.

Thus propene + HCl gives 2-chloropropane.

Reagent Product pattern / examination hook
H₂, Ni/Pt/Pd Alkane; syn delivery from the catalyst surface
Br₂ in CCl₄ Vicinal dibromide; orange colour discharged — test for unsaturation. Addition is anti through a bromonium ion
HBr, no peroxide Markovnikov bromide (ionic path)
HBr, peroxide/ROOR Anti-Markovnikov bromide (radical path); the peroxide effect is special to HBr
Conc. H₂SO₄, then warm H₂O; or H₂O/H⁺ Markovnikov alcohol by carbocation capture/rearrangement risk
1. B₂H₆; 2. H₂O₂/OH⁻ (hydroboration–oxidation) Anti-Markovnikov, syn alcohol without a free carbocation (developed again in Ch. 18)
Cold dilute alkaline KMnO₄ (Baeyer) Syn vicinal diol; purple colour fades and brown MnO₂ appears — test for unsaturation
Hot concentrated KMnO₄ Oxidative cleavage: =CH₂ → CO₂, =CHR → carboxylic acid, =CR₂ → ketone
O₃, then Zn/H₂O (reductive ozonolysis) Cleaves C=C to aldehydes/ketones; joining the carbonyl carbons in reverse locates the original double bond
Heat/pressure or radical initiator; Ziegler–Natta for ethene Addition polymer (polyethene etc.)
Worked example 17.1 — one alkene, two HBr answers

Problem. Give the major product when propene reacts with HBr (i) in the dark with no peroxide and (ii) in the presence of a peroxide.

Solution. (i) Ionic addition: protonation that gives the secondary carbocation is favoured, then Br⁻ attacks it → 2-bromopropane (Markovnikov). (ii) Peroxide initiates Br•.

The bromine radical adds first so as to leave the more stable secondary carbon radical; that radical abstracts H from HBr, placing Br on the terminal carbon → 1-bromopropane (anti-Markovnikov).

Same reagents, different mechanism, opposite orientation — and the trick does not transfer to HCl or HI.

Preparation, additions and acidity of alkynes

Ethyne (acetylene) is classically prepared by dropping water on calcium carbide:

CaC₂ + 2H₂O → C₂H₂↑ + Ca(OH)₂.

It is also obtained industrially by partial oxidation/high-temperature cracking of methane.

Alkynes in general come from double dehydrohalogenation of vicinal or geminal dihalides (alcoholic KOH; the stronger NaNH₂ is often needed to finish a terminal alkyne), and from Zn dehalogenation of vicinal tetrahalides.

The old laboratory preparation 2CHCl₃ + 6Ag → C₂H₂ + 6AgCl illustrates reductive coupling of two one-carbon fragments.

Alkynes add many alkene reagents twice unless the conditions are tuned to stop halfway:

Reagent Outcome
H₂/Lindlar cis-alkene (syn, poisoned catalyst)
Na or Li, liquid NH₃ trans-alkene (dissolving-metal reduction)
H₂/Ni or Pt, excess Alkane
Br₂ (2 equivalents) Tetrabromoalkane; bromine is decolorized
HX (2 equivalents) Geminal dihalide by two Markovnikov additions
H₂O, H₂SO₄/HgSO₄ (Kucherov hydration) Enol → carbonyl: ethyne gives ethanal; propyne gives propanone; internal unsymmetrical alkynes may give ketone mixtures
O₃ then H₂O Carboxylic acids from internal carbons; terminal ≡CH is driven to CO₂/formic-acid level
Red-hot iron tube (ethyne) Cyclic trimerization to benzene (§17.3)
ammoniacal Cu(I) catalysis (ethyne) Linear coupling/polymerization products such as vinylacetylene

Terminal alkynes are carbon acids of modest strength: HC≡C–H has pKₐ ≈ 25, far more acidic than ethene (≈44) or ethane (≈50) but still vastly weaker than water (≈15.7) or alcohols.

The trend follows s-character: an sp lone pair in ⁻C≡CR is held closer to the nucleus (50% s) and is more stable than an sp² (33% s) or sp³ (25% s) lone pair.

Therefore NaNH₂ and other very strong bases form acetylides; aqueous NaOH does not meaningfully deprotonate a terminal alkyne.

Diagnostic precipitations are coordination chemistry dressed as tests. With ammoniacal AgNO₃, a terminal alkyne gives a white silver acetylide; with ammoniacal Cu₂Cl₂ it gives a red copper(I) acetylide.

Internal alkynes lack ≡C–H and give neither. Sodium metal liberates H₂ from a terminal alkyne (and from alcohols/water too, so the sample must be dry and alcohol-free before this is called a test).

Do not store dry heavy-metal acetylides: they can be shock-sensitive explosives.

Acetylene burns in oxygen at about 3100 °C, hot enough for welding/cutting; in air its flame is smoky because of the high carbon fraction.

Its compressed gas is stored dissolved in acetone in a porous cylinder filling because free acetylene can decompose explosively under pressure (Ch. 21 revisits the safety chemistry).

17.3 Aromaticity and resonance; preparation and properties of benzene

Why benzene is not “cyclohexatriene”

Kekulé's alternating double-bond hexagon explains benzene's formula C₆H₆ but not its behaviour.

Experiment says all six C–C bonds are equal at about 139 pm (between C–C 154 pm and C=C 134 pm), all angles are 120°, the molecule is planar, and it resists the addition reactions that consume ordinary alkenes.

Resonance theory draws two equivalent Kekulé contributors; molecular-orbital language places three π bonding orbitals over the whole ring. Either way, six π electrons occupy a cyclic cloud above and below the plane.

Thermochemistry measures the prize. Hydrogenating cyclohexene releases about 120 kJ mol⁻¹, so a hypothetical 1,3,5-cyclohexatriene might be expected near 360 kJ mol⁻¹.

Benzene releases only about 208 kJ mol⁻¹ on complete hydrogenation: it starts about 152 kJ mol⁻¹ lower in energy than the invented triene. That difference is its empirical resonance (aromatic stabilization) energy.

Hückel's rule generalizes the pattern for a monocyclic system: cyclic + planar + fully conjugated + 4n+2 π electrons (n = 0, 1, 2, …) → aromatic. Benzene has 6 (n=1); naphthalene's fused 10π perimeter fits the same count.

The cyclopentadienyl anion (two π bonds + a lone pair = 6) is aromatic, explaining cyclopentadiene's unusual acidity for a hydrocarbon.

Pyrrole's nitrogen lone pair is part of its sextet, whereas pyridine's lone pair lies outside the π system and remains basic.

A planar fully conjugated 4n π system is antiaromatic; failure of planarity/conjugation makes a molecule simply non-aromatic.

Preparation of benzene

  • Cyclic trimerization: 3C₂H₂ passed through a red-hot iron/copper tube gives C₆H₆.
  • Decarboxylation: sodium benzoate with soda lime gives benzene: C₆H₅CO₂Na + NaOH → C₆H₆ + Na₂CO₃.
  • From phenol: distilling phenol with zinc dust removes oxygen: C₆H₅OH + Zn → C₆H₆ + ZnO.
  • Aromatization/reforming: n-hexane over Cr₂O₃/Al₂O₃ or Pt at high temperature gives C₆H₁₄ → C₆H₆ + 4H₂; petroleum reformate and coal tar are industrial sources.

Benzene is a colourless, volatile, flammable liquid (b.p. 80.1 °C, m.p. 5.5 °C), lighter than and almost insoluble in water, with a sweet odour.

Modern safety practice treats it as a proven human carcinogen associated with leukaemia; smelling it as a “test” belongs to history. In air it burns with a very sooty flame:

2C₆H₆ + 15O₂ → 12CO₂ + 6H₂O.

Chemical properties: substitution protects the sextet

If bromine simply added across one “double bond”, the product would surrender aromatic stabilization.

Instead benzene's π cloud attacks a strong electrophile, forming a resonance-stabilized arenium ion (σ complex); a base then removes the proton from the same carbon and the aromatic ring is restored.

Overall this is electrophilic aromatic substitution, not addition.

Reaction Conditions / electrophile Product Notes
Nitration Conc. HNO₃ + conc. H₂SO₄, about 50–55 °C; NO₂⁺ Nitrobenzene Gateway to aniline (Ch. 20); hotter mixed acid forces further substitution
Bromination/chlorination Br₂/FeBr₃ or Cl₂/FeCl₃ (or Fe) in the dark; polarized X₂–Lewis acid Bromobenzene/chlorobenzene Benzene alone does not discharge Br₂ water — the catalyst is the point
Sulfonation Fuming H₂SO₄ (SO₃) Benzenesulfonic acid Reversible; used as a removable blocking/solubilizing group
Friedel–Crafts alkylation RCl/AlCl₃ Alkylbenzene Carbocation rearrangement and polyalkylation can spoil an otherwise easy plan
Friedel–Crafts acylation RCOCl/AlCl₃ Aryl ketone, e.g. phenylethanone Product ring is deactivated, so reaction usually stops at one acyl group

Under forcing conditions addition can be compelled: hydrogenation with Ni at high temperature/pressure gives cyclohexane (C₆H₆ + 3H₂ → C₆H₁₂), and chlorine under UV adds to give hexachlorocyclohexane isomers, C₆H₆Cl₆ (the γ-isomer is lindane, now heavily restricted as a persistent pollutant).

Ozonolysis attacks all three formal π bonds and, after workup, glyoxal fragments are obtained — useful historically as evidence for the ring, not a preparative method.

For a ring that already carries a substituent, the first group steers the second. The school map (mechanism generalities from Ch. 16) is:

Existing group type Rate vs benzene Main orientation
Strong/moderate donors: –NH₂, –OH, –OR, –NHCOR Activating ortho/para
Alkyl groups Weakly activating ortho/para
Halogens Deactivating (−I stronger overall) ortho/para (+R controls position)
Strong withdrawers: –NO₂, –CN, –CHO, –COR, –CO₂H, –SO₃H Deactivating meta
Benzene and the bromine-water test

Benzene's formula is highly unsaturated (DU = 4), yet it does not decolorize bromine water or cold alkaline KMnO₄ under alkene-test conditions.

DU counts rings and π bonds; it does not say those π electrons are available for ordinary addition. Aromatic stabilization is exactly the energy that would be lost.

Common mistake

Five swaps the paper sets: alcoholic KOH eliminates (alkene), aqueous KOH substitutes (alcohol) — the solvent chooses the path; Markovnikov is the ionic rule, the peroxide effect its radical exception, and the exception works for HBr only (HCl and HI chains fail energetically); ozonolysis with Zn/H₂O stops at aldehydes and ketones; oxidative workup pushes on to acids; terminal alkynes answer silver and copper ammoniates, internal ones stay silent — and terminal alkynes are the acidic hydrocarbons, not the reactive ones; and benzene substitutes to keep its resonance energy; addition (BHC, cyclohexane) needs light, heat and excess reagent.

Identifying an alkene from reductive ozonolysis products

Problem. Reductive ozonolysis (\text{O}_3 followed by \text{Zn/H}_2\text{O}) of an alkene \text{C}_5\text{H}_{10} gives an equimolar mixture of acetone (\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3) and acetaldehyde (\text{CH}_3\text{CHO}).

Deduce the structure and IUPAC name of the alkene.

Solution. Erase the two \text{=O} oxygen atoms and join the carbonyl carbons by a double bond: (\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C=O} + \text{O=CHCH}_3 \Longrightarrow (\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C=CHCH}_3, which is 2-methylbut-2-ene.

Chapter summary

  • Refineries crack long chains, pyrolyse feedstocks to light alkenes and reform straight chains into branched/aromatic molecules that engines and polymer plants actually want.
  • Octane rewards resistance to autoignition; cetane rewards prompt compression ignition. Molecular shape therefore wins opposite prizes in the two fuels.
  • Alkanes are strong-σ, nonpolar and slow to react except by combustion and radical pathways; ethane exemplifies combustion, UV substitution and cracking.
  • Alkenes spend a π bond in addition reactions. Carbocation stability explains Markovnikov orientation, while peroxide changes HBr addition into a radical anti-Markovnikov process.
  • Alkynes can be stopped at a cis- or trans-alkene by choosing the reduction system; their terminal C–H is acidic because an sp conjugate base is comparatively stable.
  • Benzene is stabilized by a six-electron cyclic π system (Hückel 4n+2), so electrophiles substitute a ring hydrogen rather than permanently adding and destroying aromaticity.

Model answer D1: alkenes and alkynes (10 marks)

Introduction. Alkenes (\text{C}_n\text{H}_{2n}) have a C=C bond (1\sigma + 1\pi, sp², 120^{\circ}) and alkynes (\text{C}_n\text{H}_{2n-2}) have a C≡C bond (1\sigma + 2\pi, sp, 180^{\circ}).

The \pi electrons make them nucleophilic, so they undergo electrophilic addition.

Preparation. Alkenes: dehydration of alcohols with conc.

H₂SO₄ at 443\ \text{K} (Saytzeff product), dehydrohalogenation of haloalkanes with alcoholic KOH, and partial hydrogenation of alkynes with Lindlar's catalyst (cis) or Na/liquid NH₃ (trans).

Ethyne: \text{CaC}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \to \text{C}_2\text{H}_2 + \text{Ca(OH)}_2, and from 1,2-dibromoethane with alcoholic KOH.

Reactions of alkenes.

  1. Hydrogenation (Ni, 200^{\circ}\text{C}, Sabatier-Senderens): alkane.
  2. Halogenation (Br₂ in CCl₄): decolourised, the test for unsaturation, giving a vicinal dibromide by the cyclic bromonium ion.
  3. Addition of HX, Markovnikov's rule: the hydrogen of HX goes to the carbon with more hydrogens, so propene + HBr gives 2-bromopropane through the more stable 2^{\circ} carbocation.
  4. Peroxide (Kharasch) effect: with peroxides, HBr adds in the anti-Markovnikov way (free-radical chain) to give 1-bromopropane. It does not happen with HCl or HI.
  5. Hydration: acid-catalysed gives the Markovnikov alcohol, and hydroboration-oxidation gives the anti-Markovnikov alcohol.
  6. Oxidation: cold dilute alkaline KMnO₄ (Baeyer's reagent) gives a diol and decolourises the purple colour; hot KMnO₄ cleaves the bond.
  7. Ozonolysis: O₃ then Zn/H₂O gives carbonyl compounds and locates the double bond. Propene gives \text{CH}_3\text{CHO} + \text{HCHO}.

Alkynes. Terminal alkynes are weakly acidic (\text{p}K_a \approx 25, since sp carbon is most electronegative) and give a white precipitate with ammoniacal AgNO₃ and a red one with Cu₂Cl₂, which distinguishes them from alkenes and from internal alkynes.

Hydration with HgSO₄/H₂SO₄ gives a ketone (acetaldehyde from ethyne itself) by keto-enol tautomerism.

Test Ethane Ethene Ethyne
Br₂ / CCl₄ no change decolourised decolourised
Baeyer's reagent no change decolourised decolourised
Tollens' reagent (ammoniacal AgNO₃) no no white precipitate
Burning blue, clean luminous, smoky very sooty

Numerical. Complete combustion: \text{C}_2\text{H}_4 + 3\text{O}_2 \to 2\text{CO}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}. 10\ \text{mL} of ethene needs 30\ \text{mL} of O₂ and gives 20\ \text{mL} of CO₂ (at the same T and P).

For ethyne, 10\ \text{mL} needs 25\ \text{mL} of O₂. The number of \sigma and \pi bonds in propyne (\text{CH}_3\text{C}\equiv\text{CH}) is 6\sigma and 2\pi.

Conclusion. Alkenes undergo electrophilic addition by Markovnikov's rule, except HBr with peroxide, and terminal alkynes are further distinguished by their acidic hydrogen.

Model answer D2: benzene, aromaticity and electrophilic substitution (10 marks)

Introduction. Benzene, C₆H₆, is a planar hexagon of six sp² carbons with all C-C bonds equal (139\ \text{pm}, between 154 and 134). The six p electrons are delocalised above and below the ring and benzene is a resonance hybrid of the two Kekulé structures.

Aromaticity (Hückel's rule). A compound is aromatic if it is cyclic, planar, completely conjugated, and has (4n + 2)\ \pi electrons (n = 0, 1, 2, \ldots).

So benzene (6), naphthalene (10), anthracene (14), the cyclopentadienyl anion (6) and pyridine are aromatic, while cyclobutadiene (4) is anti-aromatic.

Benzene prefers substitution to addition because substitution keeps the aromatic stabilisation.

Electrophilic aromatic substitution (EAS). The general mechanism: (1) generation of the electrophile E^+, (2) attack of the ring on E^+ giving the resonance-stabilised arenium ion (sigma complex), the slow step, and (3) loss of H⁺ to restore the aromatic ring.

Reaction Reagent Electrophile
Nitration conc. HNO₃ + conc. H₂SO₄ \text{NO}_2^+
Halogenation Cl₂ or Br₂ + FeCl₃ or FeBr₃ \text{Cl}^+, \text{Br}^+
Sulphonation fuming H₂SO₄ \text{SO}_3
Friedel-Crafts alkylation RCl + anhydrous AlCl₃ \text{R}^+
Friedel-Crafts acylation RCOCl + anhydrous AlCl₃ \text{RCO}^+

Directing effects of substituents.

  1. Activating, ortho/para directing (electron-donating): -\text{OH}, -\text{NH}_2, -\text{OR}, -\text{CH}_3 and other alkyl groups.
  2. Deactivating, meta directing (electron-withdrawing): -\text{NO}_2, -\text{CN}, -\text{CHO}, -\text{COOH}, -\text{SO}_3\text{H}, -\text{NR}_3^+.
  3. Deactivating but ortho/para directing: the halogens, because of strong -I but weak +M.

Friedel-Crafts reactions fail with strongly deactivated rings (nitrobenzene) and with -\text{NH}_2 (which complexes with AlCl₃). Alkylation can rearrange the carbocation, so acylation followed by reduction gives the straight-chain product.

Other reactions. Addition of H₂ (Ni, 450\ \text{K}) gives cyclohexane and of Cl₂ (sunlight) gives hexachlorocyclohexane (BHC, gammexane). Ozonolysis of benzene gives 3 glyoxal. Combustion gives a sooty flame.

Numerical. Nitration of toluene gives about 58\% ortho, 4\% meta and 38\% para, so the o/p isomers make up about 96\%.

The theoretical yield of nitrobenzene from 7.8\ \text{g} of benzene (0.1\ \text{mol}) is 0.1\ \text{mol} = 12.3\ \text{g} (molar mass 123); at an 80\% yield 9.84\ \text{g} is obtained.

Conclusion. Benzene follows Hückel's rule and is stable, so it undergoes electrophilic substitution, and the substituent present decides the position of the next group.
